subsystems.name: Building blocks
subsystems.role: the raw molecular feedstock from which everything is made, delivered in a controlled vacuum or liquid.

subsystems.name: Positional assembly tool
subsystems.role: holds and places individual atoms or molecules with sub-nanometre precision.
parts: scanning tunnelling or atomic force microscope tip

subsystems.name: Assembler
subsystems.role: the hypothetical machine that guides chemical reactions mechanically, in the way a ribosome guides protein synthesis.

subsystems.name: Structural material
subsystems.role: the load-bearing output — carbon lattices with strength far above steel.

subsystems.name: Error detection and correction
subsystems.role: checks each placement and removes or redoes mistakes.

subsystems.name: Hierarchical assembly and scale-up
subsystems.role: grows from nanometre units to centimetre and metre structural members at useful rates.

subsystems.name: Design compiler
subsystems.role: turns a finished structure into an ordered list of assembly operations.

buildSteps.title: Design the structure atom by atom
buildSteps.detail: The target object is specified as a covalent blueprint, and software converts it into a sequence of bond-forming and placement operations.

buildSteps.title: Prepare pure feedstock
buildSteps.detail: Reagent molecules are synthesised and purified so that only the intended reactions can occur.

buildSteps.title: Do mechanosynthesis
buildSteps.detail: A scanning probe tip is used to make and break selected bonds one at a time. This has been done for individual atoms and small molecules, but only in ultra-high vacuum at very low temperature and extremely slowly.

buildSteps.title: Build a true assembler
buildSteps.detail: The step that does not yet exist: a machine that performs those reactions repeatedly without a human operator moving a tip for each atom, and that can be powered and controlled.

buildSteps.title: Replicate the assembler
buildSteps.detail: Productivity would depend on assemblers making copies of themselves, multiplying the number of build sites — a step requiring strict containment and failure controls to avoid runaway replication.

buildSteps.title: Grow and place nanotubes
buildSteps.detail: Carbon nanotubes and graphene are synthesised, sorted by size and handedness, then positioned as the structural building blocks — today done in solution and on surfaces, not in ordered macroscopic lattices.

buildSteps.title: Assemble hierarchically
buildSteps.detail: Nanotubes are bundled, cross-linked and woven into fibres, sheets and trusses, each level adding stiffness and strength while preserving atomic order.

buildSteps.title: Integrate and finish
buildSteps.detail: Wiring, thermal paths, joints and interfaces to conventional engineering systems are added, and the finished part is tested for defects.

buildSteps.title: Correct errors at every level
buildSteps.detail: Each stage uses local measurement and a rework loop, because a misplaced atom in a structural member becomes a crack. No large-scale, low-cost version of this quality control yet exists.

prerequisites.why: individual atoms and small molecules have been positioned and reacted with scanning probes, but only in vacuum, at cryogenic temperatures, and far too slowly to make anything structural.
DNA origami and block copolymers build precise nanoscale patterns, but from soft materials and not in the strong covalent lattices a building needs.
carbon nanotubes can be grown, but controlling their diameter, chirality and placement at scale is unresolved.
protein and nanoscale machine design is advancing, yet predicting and simulating a working assembler remains far out of reach.
there is no demonstrated way to build macroscopic objects with near-perfect atomic order at useful speed and cost.

pathway.milestone: single-atom manipulation and single-molecule reactions in vacuum, plus self-assembled DNA and polymer nanostructures
pathway.unlocks: the chemical rules and tooling for controlled, position-specific reactions.

pathway.milestone: molecular machines that perform repetitive, powered reaction cycles, and parallel probe arrays
pathway.unlocks: making atomically precise objects faster than one atom per operator-hour.

pathway.milestone: atomically precise sub-micron components such as molecular bearings and ordered nanotube arrays
pathway.unlocks: proof that rigid, defect-free parts can be assembled from the bottom up.

pathway.milestone: hierarchical assembly into centimetre-scale structural members
pathway.unlocks: structural materials and machine parts competitive with conventional manufacturing.

pathway.milestone: general-purpose molecular manufacturing producing metred structures on demand
pathway.unlocks: the 'instant architecture' vision — which may prove physically possible but is not a demonstrated or scheduled capability.
